overview: This bill expands several federal programs that help Western states store and manage water during droughts, run by the Interior Department's Bureau of Reclamation. It lets an existing water storage assistance program fund projects in any of the 17 Western 'Reclamation States,' makes certain projects already approved for study under the 2021 infrastructure law eligible for construction funding, and allows the department to study federally owned or state-led storage projects. It extends a small water storage grant program from five to ten years and redefines eligible projects to include both small reservoirs and groundwater recharge projects, which refill underground aquifers, within set size ranges. It also creates new grants, covering up to half the cost, for 'natural' water projects such as restoring floodplains or wetlands to hold water and recharge aquifers. The bill requires money to be spread across multiple states and says it does not override state water law or water rights. As of September 17, 2026, a Senate committee had approved it with changes and it was placed on the Senate calendar for possible floor action.
for: Supporters say the West needs every tool to store water during wet years for use in dry ones, and this gives communities more flexible options, from reservoirs to natural aquifer recharge, while respecting state water rights.
against: Critics say the bill broadens federal funding commitments for water projects without new limits on total cost, and that some natural retention projects may deliver uncertain or hard-to-measure water benefits.
